Zhang Xiaoxiao.lab_name: Guangzhou Aier Eye Hospital, Jinan University (Guangzhou, China)
Zhang Xiaoxiao.role: Eye specialist at Guangzhou Aier Eye Hospital who works on childhood myopia, from school screening and myopia-control lenses to the biology of the sclera in animal models
Zhang Xiaoxiao.sub: Guangzhou Aier Eye Hospital, affiliated with Jinan University (PubMed affiliation 2023–2026) · Optometry and Strabismus Department (2023)
story: Myopia (short-sightedness) usually happens because the eyeball grows too long. The sclera, the tough white outer wall of the eye, has to remodel for that to happen. Xiaoxiao Zhang was senior author of the 2026 FASEB Journal study in this Atlas (WEN2026), which used human scleral cells and guinea pigs whose eyes were covered to induce myopia. Too much autophagy in the sclera, the cell's recycling system, appeared to link low-oxygen stress to the remodelling. Rapamycin injected under the conjunctiva made the myopia worse, the autophagy blocker 3-MA eased it, and atropine eye drops slowed it. The team measured AMPK/mTOR/P70S6K signalling, but the paper does not show that this route causes the effect, and the results come from cells and animals, not children.

A companion 2026 paper from the same Guangzhou group, again with Zhang as last author, traced the low-oxygen signal one step further: in hypoxic scleral cells and in guinea pigs, the HIF-1alpha protein pushed cells towards glycolysis and lactate production, and blocking glycolysis reduced myopic eye growth.

Much of Zhang's other published work is clinical. PubMed lists papers from Guangzhou Aier Eye Hospital on a vision screening of more than 170,000 primary school pupils in three Guangzhou districts (2025), on predicting eye growth in children wearing orthokeratology night lenses over six years (2025), on comparing two kinds of myopia-control spectacle lenses (2023), and on eyelid hygiene during orthokeratology (2026). The hospital is affiliated with Jinan University.

highlights.WEN2026: Senior author: led the guinea pig and scleral cell study linking excess scleral autophagy to myopia, in which rapamycin worsened and 3-MA eased experimental myopia.

Zhang Xiaoxiao.note: No official staff page found; position derived from PubMed affiliations only. A 2022 case report by a Xiao-Xiao Zhang at Shanghai Children's Hospital was not counted (likely a different person).

Dan L.lab_name: School of Pharmacy, Chengdu University (Chengdu, Sichuan, China)
Dan L.role: Yeast geneticist at Chengdu University who studies reversible mutations that let cells switch drug resistance on and off, using rapamycin resistance in fission yeast as the model
Dan L.sub: School of Pharmacy and Antibiotics Innovation and Resistance Control Key Laboratory of Sichuan Province, Chengdu University (PubMed affiliation 2025–2026) · Life Sciences Institute, Zhejiang University, Hangzhou (Xiangwei He lab, PubMed affiliation 2021)
story: Fission yeast is a single-celled fungus used to study how cells control growth. Its TORC1 complex is the yeast version of mTORC1, the growth-control complex, and it can be blocked with rapamycin plus caffeine. Lufeng Dan is first author of the 2026 Microbiology Spectrum study in this Atlas (DAN2026). Some yeast cells became resistant to the drugs, then lost the resistance again a few generations later. The team showed that this was not an epigenetic switch. Mutations that broke the gaf1 gene appeared under drug pressure and then reverted to the normal DNA sequence when the drug was gone. Gaf1 is a GATA transcription factor that slows growth downstream of TORC1. The authors warn that such hidden switches can quietly change laboratory yeast stocks.

The paper continues a line of work Dan began at the Life Sciences Institute of Zhejiang University in Hangzhou, in the group of Xiangwei He. A 2021 PNAS paper with Dan as first author found drug-resistance mutations in fission yeast that are made by short tandem duplications of DNA and then flip back to the original sequence, and used deep genome sequencing to find thousands of such duplications in a single population.

By 2025 Dan was at the School of Pharmacy of Chengdu University, where a paper in the Chinese journal Hereditas described a screen that isolated 14 yeast strains with unstable rapamycin resistance, again with Xiangwei He as a co-author.

highlights.DAN2026: First author: showed that on-and-off resistance to TORC1 inhibitors in fission yeast comes from reversible mutations in gaf1.

Dan L.note: Current position inferred from 2025-2026 PubMed affiliations; no official staff page found. A 2026 temsirolimus paper by 'Lifeng Dan' (Chongqing urology) is a different person and was not used. Previous profile used 'him'; pronoun removed because no source states it.

Chresta CM.lab_name: Oncology iMed, AstraZeneca, Alderley Park (Macclesfield, England, United Kingdom)
Chresta CM.role: Cancer biologist at AstraZeneca who led the preclinical description of AZD8055, one of the first ATP-competitive mTOR kinase inhibitors to reach clinical testing
Chresta CM.sub: Oncology iMed, AstraZeneca, Alderley Park (PubMed affiliation 2009–2016, at the time of the study) · School of Biological Sciences, University of Manchester (1996, with John Hickman)
story: Rapamycin does not block mTOR completely. It sticks to the side of the enzyme and blocks only some outputs of mTORC1, and it leaves mTORC2, the second mTOR complex, largely untouched. Christine Chresta was first author of the 2009 Cancer Research paper in this Atlas (CHR2009) that described AZD8055, a drug that plugs the ATP pocket of mTOR, the site where the enzyme takes up its energy source. AZD8055 therefore blocks both complexes, including the outputs that resist rapamycin. In cancer cells and in mouse tumour models it slowed growth. The result was in cells and animals, not patients.

Chresta was one of the AstraZeneca scientists on a 2009 Biochemical Journal paper with Dario Alessi's group in Dundee describing Ku-0063794, another selective mTOR kinase inhibitor, and on a 2012 study combining AZD8055 with the MEK inhibitor selumetinib in mouse models of lung and colorectal cancer.

Earlier, at the University of Manchester, Chresta worked with John Hickman on how p53 and apoptosis, the cell's programmed death, shape the response of tumours to chemotherapy (1996 and 1999). Later AstraZeneca papers place the author in Oncology iMed at Alderley Park, working on molecular subtypes of lung and colorectal cancer (2013 to 2016). A current position could not be confirmed.

highlights.CHR2009: First author: described AZD8055, an ATP-competitive mTOR kinase inhibitor that blocks both mTORC1 and mTORC2 and slows tumour growth in mice.

Chresta CM.note: No official current profile found; last confirmed AstraZeneca affiliation is 2016. The 2009 Dundee paper (Ku-0063794, PMID 19402821) is now tied to Chresta through co-authors Cosulich and AstraZeneca; curator may add it to her timeline if it is in the Atlas.

Cosulich S.lab_name: Oncology R&D, AstraZeneca (Cambridge, England, United Kingdom)
Cosulich S.role: Cancer drug discovery scientist at AstraZeneca whose work spans PI3K and mTOR pathway inhibitors, PARP1 inhibitors and phosphoinositide lipid signalling
Cosulich S.sub: Oncology R&D, AstraZeneca, Cambridge (PubMed affiliation 2019–2026; Projects Group, 2022) · AstraZeneca, Alderley Park, Macclesfield (2009–2016)
story: Cancer cells can escape mTOR-blocking drugs by mutating mTOR itself. Sabina Cosulich is a co-author of the 2016 Nature paper in this Atlas (ROD2016), led from Memorial Sloan Kettering and UCSF, which found such mutations in breast cancer cells treated with mTOR inhibitors. Some mutations raised mTOR's own activity. The team then built RapaLink-1, a third-generation drug that joins rapamycin to an ATP-site inhibitor in one molecule, and showed in cells and mice that it still works against the resistant mutants. Cosulich was the AstraZeneca contributor on the author list.

Cosulich has worked on the mTOR pathway at AstraZeneca for many years. A 2009 Biochemical Journal paper with Dario Alessi's group in Dundee, describing the selective mTOR kinase inhibitor Ku-0063794, lists Sabina C. Cosulich together with AstraZeneca colleague Christine Chresta.

Later papers place Cosulich in AstraZeneca Oncology R&D in Cambridge, UK: on a 2019 review and a 2025 study with the Babraham Institute about the fatty-acid make-up of phosphoinositides, the membrane lipids that PI3K signalling uses, on the 2022 preclinical description of the PARP1 inhibitor AZD5305, and on a 2026 paper about a TEAD inhibitor for Hippo-pathway cancers.

highlights.ROD2016: Co-author: AstraZeneca contributor to the study that found mTOR resistance mutations and designed RapaLink-1 to overcome them.

Cosulich S.note: Current position based on 2026 PubMed affiliation (AstraZeneca, Cambridge); no official profile page found. Previous profile used 'her'; pronoun removed because no source states it.

Kraig E.lab_name: Department of Cell Systems and Anatomy, UT Health San Antonio (San Antonio, Texas, USA)
Kraig E.role: Immunologist at UT Health San Antonio who studies how aging changes immune regulation and who led the first small safety trial of rapamycin in healthy older people at the Barshop Institute
Kraig E.sub: Professor and Deputy Chair of Faculty Development, Department of Cell Systems and Anatomy, UT Health San Antonio · Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies · Distinguished Fellow, American Association of Immunologists · postdoc, Leroy Hood lab, Caltech · PhD, Brandeis University (Jim Haber lab)
story: Before anyone can test whether rapamycin slows human aging, someone has to show that healthy older people can take it safely. Ellen Kraig was first author of the 2018 trial in this Atlas (KRA2018) that asked this question. Twenty-five healthy adults aged 70 to 95 took low-dose rapamycin or a placebo every day for at least 8 weeks. The drug was generally well tolerated. There were small changes in red blood cell measures and no rise in blood glucose or insulin resistance. The trial was small and short, so it says nothing about long-term benefit, but it was early groundwork for larger aging trials.

Kraig trained in genetics and immunology. As a graduate student at Brandeis University in Jim Haber's lab Kraig studied mating type in yeast, and then joined Leroy Hood's lab at Caltech as a postdoc. At UT Health San Antonio Kraig is Professor and Deputy Chair of Faculty Development in the Department of Cell Systems and Anatomy. Kraig's research uses molecular and cellular assays to study how aging affects immune regulation, work developed with colleagues at the Barshop Institute. Kraig has also won several teaching awards, including a 2018 Regents' Outstanding Teaching Award, and was named a Distinguished Fellow of the American Association of Immunologists.

The question from the pilot trial continues. In 2026 UT Health San Antonio announced a larger randomized, placebo-controlled study of rapamycin and everolimus in about 84 healthy adults aged 65 to 90, co-led by Kraig with Dean Kellogg Jr. and Brett Ginsburg, to work out dosing and short-term effects in older people.

highlights.KRA2018: First author: ran the randomized pilot trial showing that daily low-dose rapamycin was well tolerated by healthy adults aged 70 to 95 over 8 weeks.

Kraig E.note: No third-person pronouns used; the UT System award page is written in first person. lab_url is the official UT System award profile, not a lab page.

Musi N.lab_name: Diabetes and Aging Center, Cedars-Sinai Medical Center (Los Angeles, California, USA)
Musi N.role: Endocrinologist and aging researcher who directs the Division of Endocrinology, Diabetes and Metabolism and the Diabetes and Aging Center at Cedars-Sinai, and who studies how aging drives insulin resistance, frailty and senescence
Musi N.sub: Director, Division of Endocrinology, Diabetes and Metabolism, and Director, Diabetes and Aging Center, Cedars-Sinai Medical Center (since 2022) · Kathi and Gary Cypres Chair in Diabetes Research (2024) · earlier at the Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies, UT Health San Antonio, and South Texas Veterans Health Care System (PubMed affiliation 2018)
story: Nicolas Musi is a co-author of the 2018 trial in this Atlas (KRA2018), a randomized placebo-controlled pilot study in 25 healthy adults aged 70 to 95. Daily low-dose rapamycin for at least 8 weeks was generally well tolerated, with small changes in red blood cell measures and no rise in blood glucose or insulin resistance. That last point matters because rapamycin can disturb sugar handling in mice. The trial was small and short.

At the time Musi worked at the Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies and the Department of Medicine of UT Health San Antonio, and at the South Texas Veterans Health Care System. Musi's research covers how aging affects metabolism and cells in diabetes, obesity and sarcopenia (age-related muscle loss), the effects of exercise on glucose and fat metabolism, and cellular senescence, the state in which damaged cells stop dividing but stay active.

Musi moved to Cedars-Sinai Medical Center in Los Angeles in 2022. There Musi directs the Division of Endocrinology, Diabetes and Metabolism and the Diabetes and Aging Center, and in 2024 became the first holder of the Kathi and Gary Cypres Chair in Diabetes Research. The current work includes a clinical trial testing whether removing senescent cells improves glucose metabolism and physical function. Musi is an elected member of the Academy for Health and Lifespan Research.

highlights.KRA2018: Co-author: part of the San Antonio team that ran the pilot safety trial of daily rapamycin in healthy adults aged 70 to 95.

Musi N.note: Text avoids pronouns. Training (MD school, fellowship) not found in an official source. ZHO2001 (initial N only) still not linked.

Fernandez E.lab_name: Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies, UT Health San Antonio (San Antonio, Texas, USA)
Fernandez E.role: Aging researcher at the Barshop Institute in San Antonio who has worked on rapamycin studies in mice and common marmosets, including the NIA Interventions Testing Program
Fernandez E.sub: Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies, UT Health San Antonio, and Geriatric Research, Education and Clinical Center, South Texas Veterans Health Care System (PubMed affiliation 2014–2026) · Department of Pharmacology, UT Health San Antonio
story: Rapamycin lengthens life in mice, but mice are far from people. Elizabeth Fernandez is a co-author of two Atlas studies that tried the drug in the common marmoset, a small, short-lived monkey. The 2014 study (TAR2014) worked out how to give rapamycin by mouth in a coated form, reached blood levels similar to those in mouse and human work, and saw lower mTORC1 signalling, the growth-control pathway, in the animals' tissues. The 2015 study (ROS2015) found that long-term treatment had only minor effects on body weight, activity, blood fats and glucose handling. Neither study measured lifespan.

Fernandez is also a co-author of a 2022 report from the NIA Interventions Testing Program (STR2022), which tests possible anti-aging drugs in genetically mixed mice at three sites. Rapamycin combined with acarbose, a diabetes drug, gave male mice a longer lifespan than rapamycin alone had in earlier cohorts. In females the combination was no better than rapamycin alone.

PubMed places Fernandez at the Barshop Institute, UT Health San Antonio, and at the Geriatric Research, Education and Clinical Center of the South Texas Veterans Health Care System on papers from 2014 to 2026. A 2026 paper with Randy Strong found that long-term rapamycin protected aging mice against the decline in motor function, with a larger effect in females. A current job title could not be confirmed from an official page.

highlights.TAR2014: Co-author: part of the team that first described oral rapamycin dosing, blood levels and mTORC1 inhibition in common marmosets.
highlights.ROS2015: Co-author: contributed to the study showing that long-term rapamycin had only minor metabolic effects in marmosets.
highlights.STR2022: Co-author: contributed to the Interventions Testing Program report in which rapamycin plus acarbose extended male mouse lifespan beyond rapamycin alone.

Fernandez E.note: No official profile found. Previous profile used 'her'; pronoun removed because no source states it. Five more Atlas records under this name lack PubMed affiliation and remain unlinked.

Lelegren M.lab_name: Geriatric Research, Education and Clinical Center, South Texas Veterans Health Care System, and Barshop Institute, UT Health San Antonio (San Antonio, Texas, USA)
Lelegren M.role: First author of a 2016 study of how rapamycin changes the protein-quality-control machinery in marmoset liver, muscle and fat, carried out in Adam Salmon's group in San Antonio
Lelegren M.sub: Geriatric Research, Education and Clinical Center, South Texas Veterans Health Care System, and Barshop Institute, UT Health San Antonio (at the time of the study, 2016)
story: Cells keep their proteins in good shape with a set of systems called the proteostasis network. Proteasomes chop up damaged proteins, chaperones help proteins fold, and autophagy recycles larger pieces of the cell. Blocking mTOR is thought to boost some of these systems, which may be part of how rapamycin slows aging in mice.

Matthew Lelegren was first author of the 2016 Atlas study (LEL2016) that checked this idea in a primate, using tissue from common marmosets treated with rapamycin in an earlier pilot. In liver and muscle, rapamycin went with more of PSMB5, a core proteasome subunit, but proteasome activity did not change. Chaperones that work inside mitochondria rose in muscle but not liver, and autophagy rose in muscle and fat but not liver. Only parts of the network responded, and differently in each tissue. The samples came from a small group of animals, and the changes are protein levels, not proven effects on health.

The work was done at the South Texas Veterans Health Care System and the Barshop Institute in San Antonio, with Adam Salmon as senior author. No later research paper tied to this person could be confirmed, so the current position is not known.

highlights.LEL2016: First author: measured proteasome, chaperone and autophagy markers in rapamycin-treated marmoset tissues and found tissue-specific changes.

Lelegren M.note: PubMed lists a Matthew (J.) Lelegren in Otolaryngology at Eastern Virginia Medical School, Norfolk (2020-2022, PMIDs 33170026, 33934006, 35985081). The name is rare and the career path (research in San Antonio, then medical training) is plausible, but there is no shared institution or co-author, so it was NOT used. Curator may want to confirm.

Ross C.lab_name: Ross Lab, Southwest National Primate Research Center, Texas Biomedical Research Institute (San Antonio, Texas, USA)
Ross C.role: Primate biologist at Texas Biomedical Research Institute who uses the common marmoset to test whether drugs such as rapamycin can protect health during aging
Ross C.sub: Professor and Principal Investigator, Texas Biomedical Research Institute · Associate Director for Research, Southwest National Primate Research Center · earlier at the Barshop Institute, UT Health San Antonio, and Texas A&M University San Antonio (PubMed affiliation 2014–2016) · postdoc in the Biology of Aging, UT Health San Antonio · PhD in Biological Sciences, University of Nebraska-Lincoln (2005)
story: Rapamycin extends life in mice, but no one knows yet whether it does the same in primates. The common marmoset, a small South American monkey that lives about 10 to 15 years, is a practical test case. Corinna Ross was first author of the 2015 Atlas study (ROS2015) on long-term oral rapamycin in marmosets. Body weight, daily activity, blood fats and glucose handling barely changed, so the metabolic side effects that worry people about the drug were small in these animals. In the liver, one enzyme that makes glucose (G6Pase) became less active.

Ross is also a co-author of the 2014 study that first worked out how to dose rapamycin in marmosets (TAR2014) and of the 2016 study on proteasome and autophagy changes in the same animals (LEL2016). These three papers belong to a longer San Antonio project that set up the marmoset as a model for testing anti-aging drugs.

Ross studied biology at Cornell University and the University of Nebraska Omaha, earned a PhD in biological sciences at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln in 2005, and trained as a postdoctoral Biology of Aging fellow at UT Health San Antonio. At the time of these studies PubMed lists Ross at the Barshop Institute and at Texas A&M University San Antonio. Ross now runs a laboratory as Professor at Texas Biomedical Research Institute and is Associate Director for Research at the Southwest National Primate Research Center, still using marmosets to study interventions for healthy aging.

highlights.ROS2015: First author: showed that long-term oral rapamycin had only minor metabolic effects in common marmosets.
highlights.TAR2014: Co-author: part of the team that first described rapamycin dosing, blood levels and mTORC1 inhibition in marmosets.
highlights.LEL2016: Co-author: contributed marmoset tissue work to the study of proteasome, chaperone and autophagy changes under rapamycin.

Ross C.note: Texas Biomed page uses she/her, but the text avoids pronouns. Full name with middle initial (Corinna N. Ross) from PubMed 2025.

Tardif S.lab_name: Southwest National Primate Research Center, Texas Biomedical Research Institute (San Antonio, Texas, USA)
Tardif S.role: Primate biologist who spent more than 30 years developing the common marmoset as a research model, and who led the first studies of rapamycin dosing and safety in this small monkey
Tardif S.sub: Scientist and Associate Director of Primate Research, Texas Biomedical Research Institute · Associate Director of Research, Southwest National Primate Research Center · Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies, UT Health San Antonio (PubMed affiliation 2014–2016)
story: Suzette Tardif was first author of the 2014 Atlas study (TAR2014) that first described how to give rapamycin to the common marmoset. The drug was put in a protective coating and fed by mouth at about 1 mg per kg each day. Blood levels were similar to those in mouse aging studies and within the range used in human medicine. In treated animals, the marker of mTORC1 activity, the growth-control complex, fell in blood cells, liver and fat. The monkeys showed no anemia, lung scarring or mouth ulcers, side effects known from patients on the drug.

Tardif was senior author of the 2015 follow-up (ROS2015), which found only minor metabolic effects of long-term treatment, and a co-author of the 2016 study on proteasome and autophagy changes in the same animals (LEL2016). Together these papers made the marmoset a usable model for testing anti-aging drugs in a primate, though none of them measured lifespan.

Tardif's research covers metabolism, behaviour and reproduction in marmosets, and more recently their use as a model of obesity and aging. A 2025 study with Corinna Ross on predicting obesity and blood-sugar problems in adult marmosets lists Tardif at the Southwest National Primate Research Center of Texas Biomedical Research Institute, where Tardif has served as Associate Director of Research.

highlights.TAR2014: First author: first described oral rapamycin dosing, blood levels and mTORC1 inhibition in common marmosets.
highlights.ROS2015: Senior author: led the study showing only minor metabolic effects of long-term rapamycin in marmosets.
highlights.LEL2016: Co-author: provided the marmoset cohort for the study of proteasome and autophagy markers under rapamycin.

Tardif S.note: Current title from a Newswise expert profile (undated, not an institutional page, so not used as lab_url); 2025 PubMed affiliation confirms Texas Biomed/SNPRC. PhD details not found. Text avoids pronouns.

Nelson G.lab_name: Bioimaging Unit, Newcastle University (Newcastle upon Tyne, England, United Kingdom)
Nelson G.role: Microscopy specialist who manages Newcastle University's Bioimaging Unit and has worked for many years on the signalling networks that keep senescent cells in their arrested state
Nelson G.sub: Specialist Experimental Scientific Officer and manager, Bioimaging Unit, Newcastle University · postdoc with Thomas von Zglinicki, Newcastle University · postdocs at the University of Liverpool and AstraZeneca · BSc and PhD, University of Edinburgh
story: Senescent cells have stopped dividing for good but stay alive and active, and they build up in aging tissues. Glyn Nelson is a co-author of two Newcastle studies in this Atlas that look at how mTORC1, the growth-control complex, behaves in these cells. The 2017 paper (CAR2017), on which Nelson is second author, found that mTORC1 stays switched on in senescent human fibroblasts and no longer responds when nutrients or growth factors are taken away. The fault lies upstream of mTORC1, in how the cells sense amino acids and growth signals. The 2024 paper (KEL2024) found that the routine clearing of damaged mitochondria shuts down as cells become senescent or old. Both studies were done in cultured human cells.

Nelson studied at the University of Edinburgh for a BSc and a PhD, then worked as a postdoc at AstraZeneca and at the University of Liverpool, and later joined Thomas von Zglinicki's group at Newcastle, which studies cell senescence. That research thread, on the signalling networks that start and maintain senescence, continues alongside Nelson's imaging role.

Nelson now manages Newcastle University's Bioimaging Unit, which gives researchers across the university access to light microscopes, training and image analysis help. Nelson also develops standard quality-control methods for light microscopy with the international QUAREP-LiMi initiative.

highlights.CAR2017: Second author: contributed to the study showing that mTORC1 stays active in senescent human cells because nutrient and growth-factor sensing upstream of it is faulty.
highlights.KEL2024: Co-author: contributed to the study showing that basal mitophagy shuts down in senescent and aged human cells.

Nelson G.note: Previous profile used 'him'; pronoun removed because the staff page does not state it.

Kelly G.lab_name: Korolchuk Lab, Biosciences Institute, Newcastle University (Newcastle upon Tyne, England, United Kingdom)
Kelly G.role: Cell biologist from Viktor Korolchuk's group at Newcastle University who showed that the routine clearing of damaged mitochondria fails as human cells become senescent
Kelly G.sub: Biosciences Institute, Newcastle University (PubMed affiliation 2020–2024, Korolchuk lab, at the time of the study)
story: Mitochondria are the power stations of the cell, and damaged ones are removed by a process called mitophagy. George Kelly is first author of the 2024 Developmental Cell study in this Atlas (KEL2024). In healthy primary human cells, mitophagy ran at a steady high level, started by superoxide made in the mitochondria and carried out through the PINK1/Parkin pathway with p62 as the receptor that tags mitochondria for removal. This housekeeping shut down when cells became senescent, the non-dividing state that builds up with age, and in cells from older donors. Blocking mitophagy in young cells was enough to push them into senescence.

The study also matters for rapamycin. Turning mitophagy back on was needed for rapamycin and NAD precursors to hold back senescence, which suggests that part of rapamycin's effect on cell aging works through mitochondrial quality control. A small molecule that targets p62 could restore mitophagy and reverse aging features in the cells. All of this was shown in cultured human cells.

PubMed links Kelly to Viktor Korolchuk's group at Newcastle University from 2020, starting with a review on reactive oxygen species and autophagy in neurons. Kelly is also a co-author of a 2022 Developmental Cell paper from the same lab showing that autophagy keeps cells alive by maintaining NAD levels, of a 2022 eLife study on short senolytic treatments in irradiated mice, and of a 2023 Nature paper with Joao Passos on how stressed senescent cells release mitochondrial DNA. A current position could not be confirmed.

highlights.KEL2024: First author: showed that basal mitophagy shuts down in senescent and aged human cells and that its return is needed for rapamycin's anti-senescence effect.

Kelly G.note: No staff or thesis page found; position is the PubMed affiliation up to 2024.

Nojima H.lab_name: Biosignal Research Center, Kobe University (Kobe, Japan)
Nojima H.role: First author of the 2003 Kobe study showing that raptor grabs mTOR's targets through a short TOS motif, the docking step that lets mTORC1 reach its substrates
Nojima H.sub: Biosignal Research Center, Kobe University, Kazuyoshi Yonezawa group (at the time of the study, 2003)
story: An enzyme like mTOR has to find the right proteins to act on. In 2002 two groups discovered raptor, a partner protein that sits next to mTOR in the complex now called mTORC1, the growth-control complex. One of those groups was Kazuyoshi Yonezawa's team at Kobe University. Hiroki Nojima was first author of their 2003 follow-up in the Journal of Biological Chemistry (NOJ2003).

The study showed that raptor binds two of mTOR's best-known targets, p70 S6 kinase and 4E-BP1, both of which control how fast cells make proteins. Raptor holds them through a short stretch of five amino acids called the TOS motif (TOR signalling motif). When the motif was changed, raptor could no longer bind and mTOR could no longer act on the target. This made raptor the part of mTORC1 that presents substrates to the kinase, a model that has held up in later structural work. The experiments were done in cultured cells and with purified proteins.
PubMed lists Nojima at the Biosignal Research Center of Kobe University. No other paper could be tied to this person with confidence, so later career steps are not known.

highlights.NOJ2003: First author: showed that raptor binds S6 kinase and 4E-BP1 through their TOS motifs, which lets mTORC1 present these substrates to the kinase.

Nojima H.note: Other PubMed records under 'Nojima H' belong to Hideaki Nojima (zebrafish, Osaka) and Hiroshi Nojima (Osaka); not used.

Hidayat S.lab_name: Biosignal Research Center, Kobe University (Kobe, Japan)
Hidayat S.role: Member of Kazuyoshi Yonezawa's Kobe team that co-discovered raptor and worked out how mTOR senses amino acids, and first author of a study showing that a leucine derivative can block amino acid-mTOR signalling
Hidayat S.sub: Biosignal Research Center, Kobe University, Kazuyoshi Yonezawa group (PubMed records 2000–2006, at the time of the studies)
story: In 2002 two teams, one in Boston and one in Kobe, reported raptor, the partner protein that defines mTORC1, the growth-control complex. Sujuti Hidayat is a co-author of the Kobe paper in Cell (HARA2002). It showed that raptor is needed for mTOR to act on 4E-BP1 and S6 kinase, two proteins that control protein synthesis, and that silencing raptor in the worm C. elegans mimics loss of TOR. Hidayat is also a co-author of the 2003 follow-up (NOJ2003) showing that raptor holds these targets through a short TOS motif.

Hidayat's own first-author paper from the same group, published in 2003, tested a chemical cousin of the amino acid leucine. It blocked the amino acid signal to mTOR in human Jurkat cells, a line of immune cells, and stopped them in the G1 phase of the cell cycle. That study lists Hidayat at the Biosignal Research Center of Kobe University.

PubMed records place Hidayat in the Yonezawa group from 2000 to 2006, on papers about the tail region of mTOR that the enzyme needs to work (2000), about how the Hsp90 inhibitor geldanamycin disrupts the mTOR-raptor pathway (2006), and about the two motifs of 4E-BP1 that bind raptor (2006). A current position could not be confirmed.

highlights.HARA2002: Co-author: part of the Kobe team that co-discovered raptor and showed it is needed for mTOR to act on 4E-BP1 and S6 kinase.
highlights.NOJ2003: Co-author: contributed to the study showing that raptor binds mTOR substrates through their TOS motif.

Tokunaga C.lab_name: Biosignal Research Center, Kobe University (Kobe, Japan)
Tokunaga C.role: Member of Kazuyoshi Yonezawa's Kobe team that co-discovered raptor, and first author of a 2004 review on how mTOR combines amino acid and energy signals
Tokunaga C.sub: Biosignal Research Center, Kobe University, Kazuyoshi Yonezawa group (PubMed records 2000–2006, at the time of the studies)
story: Chiharu Tokunaga is a co-author of the 2002 Cell paper from Kobe University (HARA2002) that, together with a Boston study in the same issue, reported raptor, the partner protein that defines mTORC1, the growth-control complex. The Kobe team showed that raptor is needed for mTOR to act on 4E-BP1 and S6 kinase and that silencing raptor in worms mimics loss of TOR. Tokunaga is also a co-author of the 2003 follow-up (NOJ2003), which found that raptor holds these two targets through a short TOS motif and so presents them to the kinase.

In 2004 Tokunaga was first author, with Ken-ichi Yoshino and Kazuyoshi Yonezawa, of a review in Biochemical and Biophysical Research Communications explaining how mTOR brings together two kinds of information, whether amino acids are available and whether the cell has enough energy. PubMed lists Tokunaga at the Biosignal Research Center of Kobe University on that review.

Other PubMed records from the same group, from 2000 to 2006, include work on the tail region of mTOR that the enzyme needs to work, on a leucine derivative that blocks amino acid signalling to mTOR, on how the Hsp90 inhibitor geldanamycin disrupts the mTOR-raptor pathway, and on the motifs of 4E-BP1 that bind raptor. A current position could not be confirmed.

highlights.HARA2002: Co-author: part of the Kobe team that co-discovered raptor and showed it is needed for mTOR to act on 4E-BP1 and S6 kinase.
highlights.NOJ2003: Co-author: contributed to the study showing that raptor binds mTOR substrates through their TOS motif.

Tokunaga C.note: A 2026 paper by 'Chiho Tokunaga' (Tsukuba cardiovascular surgery) is a different person and was not used.

Imseng S.lab_name: Maier Lab, Biozentrum, University of Basel (Basel, Switzerland)
Imseng S.role: Structural biologist from Timm Maier's group at the Biozentrum Basel who helped solve the first detailed structures of human mTORC1 and mTORC2 and then worked on a drug to block mTORC1 specifically
Imseng S.sub: Biozentrum, University of Basel (PubMed affiliation 2013–2021, at the time of the studies) · PhD, University of Basel (2016, thesis on the structure of mTORC1, advisors Timm Maier and Tilman Schirmer)
story: To see how a protein machine works, structural biologists try to see its shape. Stefan Imseng is a co-author of three Atlas studies that did this for the two mTOR complexes using cryo-electron microscopy, which photographs frozen protein molecules and combines thousands of images into a 3D model. The 2015 Science paper (AYL2015) showed the architecture of human mTORC1, the growth-control complex: two copies of mTOR and its partners form a diamond-shaped dimer, and the structure showed how rapamycin bound to its helper protein FKBP12 narrows the entrance to the active site. The 2018 eLife paper (STU2018) did the same for the core of mTORC2, and the 2020 Science Advances paper (SCA2020) sharpened that picture to 3.2 angstroms, showing that the end of the partner protein Rictor covers the spot where rapamycin would bind. That explains why mTORC2 resists rapamycin.

Imseng did doctoral work in Timm Maier's structural biology group at the Biozentrum. The 2016 thesis, supervised by Maier and Tilman Schirmer, was titled 'Structural studies on the target of rapamycin complex 1'. Imseng was first author of a 2018 review on the architecture and activation of the PI3K-related kinase family to which mTOR belongs, and a co-author of later Basel studies on how DEPTOR regulates both mTOR complexes (2021) and on how mTORC1 recognises its substrate 4E-BP1 (2021).

In 2018 the Biozentrum announced an Innosuisse-funded project in which Imseng and Asier Gonzalez, supported by Timm Maier and Michael Hall, set out to develop a lead compound that blocks mTORC1 specifically, as a possible drug for tuberous sclerosis. A current position could not be confirmed.

highlights.AYL2015: Co-author: part of the team that solved the cryo-EM architecture of human mTORC1, including its complex with FKBP12-rapamycin.
highlights.STU2018: Co-author: contributed to the first architecture of the human mTORC2 core complex.
highlights.SCA2020: Co-author: contributed to the 3.2 angstrom structure of human mTORC2 that pinpoints Rictor as the cause of its rapamycin insensitivity.

Imseng S.note: The Biozentrum news page uses 'his'; text avoids pronouns. Outcome of the 2018-2020 Innosuisse spin-off project not known.

Sauer E.role: Structural biologist at the Biozentrum Basel who worked on the structure of the mTOR kinase and contributed to the cryo-EM structures of human mTORC1 and mTORC2
Sauer E.sub: Biozentrum, University of Basel (PubMed affiliation 2013–2018, at the time of the studies)
story: Evelyn Sauer is a co-author of two Atlas studies from Basel that used cryo-electron microscopy to show the shape of the mTOR complexes. The 2015 Science paper (AYL2015) gave the first detailed architecture of human mTORC1, the growth-control complex, including how rapamycin bound to its helper protein FKBP12 narrows access to the active site. The 2018 eLife paper (STU2018) did the same for the core of mTORC2, made of mTOR, Rictor, SIN1 and mLST8, and helped explain why mTORC2 resists rapamycin.

Sauer was first author, with Stefan Imseng, Timm Maier and Michael Hall, of a 2013 review in Biochemical Society Transactions on the conserved sequence motifs and structure of the mTOR kinase domain, the part of the enzyme that transfers phosphate groups. Earlier Basel work by Sauer was in protein crystallography: a 2013 single-author paper on the structure and RNA binding of the bacterial protein Hfq, and a 2014 study of the cell-death regulator BCL-W solved with designed binding proteins.
PubMed lists Sauer at the Biozentrum of the University of Basel on all of these papers. A current position could not be confirmed.

highlights.AYL2015: Co-author: contributed to the cryo-EM architecture of human mTORC1.
highlights.STU2018: Co-author: contributed to the architecture of the human mTORC2 core complex.

Sauer E.note: No official page found. Ancient-DNA papers by 'Eberhard Sauer' (Edinburgh) are a different person.

Battaglioni S.lab_name: Hall Lab, Biozentrum, University of Basel (Basel, Switzerland)
Battaglioni S.role: Cell biologist in Michael Hall's group at the Biozentrum Basel, first author of a 2022 Cell review that catalogued the direct substrates of mTOR
Battaglioni S.sub: Biozentrum, University of Basel, Michael N. Hall group (PubMed affiliation 2020–2024) · Institute of Biochemistry, ETH Zurich (PubMed affiliation 2020)
story: mTOR is a kinase, an enzyme that switches other proteins on or off by attaching phosphate groups to them. Which proteins it acts on decides what mTOR does in the cell. Stefania Battaglioni is first author of the 2022 Cell review in this Atlas (BAT2022), written with Michael Hall, which gathered the known direct substrates of mTOR and explained how the two complexes, mTORC1 and mTORC2, end up acting on different targets. It is a reference map for anyone trying to trace a signal from mTOR to an effect.

Battaglioni's own lab work in the Hall group looks for new mTOR substrates. A 2024 PNAS paper, with Battaglioni as first author, showed that mTORC1 phosphorylates and stabilises a protein called LST2, which in turn holds back the EGF receptor, a growth-factor receptor. A 2023 EMBO Journal study, on which Battaglioni is a co-author, found that yeast TORC1 switches off Stm1, a factor that keeps ribosomes dormant, so that protein synthesis can restart when nutrients return.

Battaglioni also contributed to a 2020 Nature Metabolism study, led from ETH Zurich, showing that the pH inside cells helps drive cell division and tumour growth by raising cyclin D1. PubMed lists Battaglioni at the Biozentrum of the University of Basel through 2024. A current job title could not be confirmed.

highlights.BAT2022: First author: wrote, with Michael Hall, the Cell review that catalogues direct mTOR substrates and how mTORC1 and mTORC2 choose their targets.

Battaglioni S.note: No official profile page found; position from PubMed only.

Bentzinger CF.lab_name: Bentzinger Lab, Department of Pharmacology-Physiology, Université de Sherbrooke (Sherbrooke, Quebec, Canada)
Bentzinger CF.role: Muscle stem cell biologist at the Université de Sherbrooke who, as a PhD student in Basel, showed that mTORC1 but not mTORC2 is essential for healthy skeletal muscle
Bentzinger CF.sub: Professor, Department of Pharmacology-Physiology, Faculty of Medicine and Health Sciences, Université de Sherbrooke, and researcher at the CRCHUS (since 2016) · Nestlé Institute of Health Sciences, Lausanne (2014–2016) · postdoc, Ottawa Hospital Research Institute (2009–2013) · PhD, Biozentrum, University of Basel (2005–2009)
story: mTOR works in two complexes. mTORC1 needs the partner protein raptor, and mTORC2 needs rictor. Florian Bentzinger was first author of the 2008 Cell Metabolism study in this Atlas (BEN2008) from Markus Ruegg's group at the Biozentrum in Basel. The team deleted raptor or rictor only in the skeletal muscle of mice. Without raptor, the muscles changed their metabolism and developed muscular dystrophy, a progressive breakdown of muscle tissue. Without rictor, the muscles stayed normal. This showed that mTORC1, not mTORC2, is the complex that muscle depends on, a result from mice that has guided later thinking about mTOR drugs and muscle.

Bentzinger did an MSc and then a PhD at the Biozentrum of the University of Basel (2005 to 2009). From 2009 to 2013 Bentzinger was a postdoc at the Ottawa Hospital Research Institute in Canada, and from 2014 to 2016 worked at the Nestlé Institute of Health Sciences in Lausanne.

Since 2016 Bentzinger has been a professor in the Department of Pharmacology-Physiology at the Université de Sherbrooke and a researcher at its hospital research centre, the CRCHUS. The lab studies muscle stem cells and their niche, the surrounding tissue and extracellular matrix that tell the stem cells when to rest and when to rebuild muscle, and how these signals fail in aging and muscular dystrophy. The group has also developed a protocol for making muscle stem cells from induced pluripotent stem cells.

highlights.BEN2008: First author: showed in mice that losing raptor, not rictor, in skeletal muscle causes metabolic changes and muscular dystrophy.

Bentzinger CF.note: PhD supervisor not named in the official profile; BEN2008 senior author is Markus Ruegg. Postdoc supervisor (Ottawa) not stated in the source, so not named. Sherbrooke is not in canonical_locations; used '(Sherbrooke, Quebec, Canada)'. Pronoun 'him' removed.

Duran RV.lab_name: Centro Andaluz de Biología Molecular y Medicina Regenerativa (CABIMER), CSIC (Seville, Spain)
Duran RV.role: Cell biologist who showed that glutamine breakdown feeds amino acid signalling to mTORC1, and who now leads research on mTOR, glutamine metabolism and cancer at CABIMER in Seville
Duran RV.sub: Senior Researcher, Spanish National Research Council (CSIC), CABIMER, Seville · group leader, Institut Européen de Chimie et Biologie, INSERM U1218 and University of Bordeaux (PubMed affiliation 2015–2017) · postdoc, Michael N. Hall lab, Biozentrum, University of Basel (2012) · doctoral work, Instituto de Bioquímica Vegetal y Fotosíntesis, University of Seville and CSIC (2006)
story: Cells check whether they have enough amino acids before they grow, and mTORC1, the growth-control complex, is the checkpoint. Raúl Durán was first author of the 2012 Molecular Cell study in this Atlas (DUR2012), from Michael Hall's lab in Basel. In cultured cells, glutamine together with leucine switched on mTORC1 by speeding up glutaminolysis, the breakdown of glutamine into alpha-ketoglutarate. Alpha-ketoglutarate then acted through the Rag GTPases, the switches that bring mTORC1 to the lysosome. The work linked a metabolic pathway that many cancer cells overuse to the main growth signal.

Durán started in a different field. A 2006 first-author paper from the Instituto de Bioquímica Vegetal y Fotosíntesis in Seville studied how electron-carrier proteins feed photosystem I in cyanobacteria. After the postdoc in Basel, Durán led a team at the Institut Européen de Chimie et Biologie in Bordeaux (INSERM and University of Bordeaux). There the group described 'glutamoptosis', a form of cell death caused when glutaminolysis runs unchecked during nutrient shortage and autophagy is blocked (2017).

Durán is now a Senior Researcher of the Spanish National Research Council (CSIC) at CABIMER in Seville. A 2026 paper from the group, with Durán as senior author, found that the FGFR1 receptor drives a metabolic rewiring that lets glioblastoma cells resist the chemotherapy drug temozolomide, and that blocking FGFR1 restored sensitivity in cells and mouse models.

highlights.DUR2012: First author: showed in cells that glutaminolysis, through alpha-ketoglutarate, activates Rag-mTORC1 signalling.

Duran RV.note: Current position from a Frontiers Loop profile plus a 2026 PubMed affiliation (CABIMER, Seville); no institutional page opened, so no lab_url. Seville is not in canonical_locations; used '(Seville, Spain)'. Pronoun 'him' removed.

Robitaille AM.lab_name: Thermo Fisher Scientific (San Jose, California, USA)
Robitaille AM.role: Mass spectrometry scientist who, as a PhD student in Michael Hall's lab, used phosphoproteomics to show that mTORC1 switches on the cell's production of pyrimidines, and who now works on proteomics applications at Thermo Fisher Scientific
Robitaille AM.sub: Senior Product Applications Specialist, Thermo Fisher Scientific, San Jose · postdoc, Randall Moon lab, University of Washington, Seattle · PhD, Michael N. Hall lab, Biozentrum, University of Basel
story: To grow and divide, a cell must copy its DNA and make lots of RNA, and both need pyrimidines, a family of chemical building blocks. Aaron Robitaille was first author of the 2013 Science paper in this Atlas (ROB2013), from Michael Hall's lab in Basel. Using quantitative phosphoproteomics, a mass spectrometry method that measures thousands of phosphorylation sites at once, the team found 335 proteins whose phosphorylation depended on mTOR. One of them was CAD, the enzyme that runs the first three steps of making pyrimidines. mTORC1, the growth-control complex, switches CAD on through S6 kinase. The work, done in cultured cells, tied the main growth signal directly to the supply of DNA and RNA building blocks.

Robitaille did the PhD at the University of Basel in Michael Hall's laboratory and then moved to the University of Washington in Seattle as a postdoc in Randall Moon's lab, using quantitative proteomics to measure protein levels and protein partners and to find regulators of embryonic stem cell differentiation. The thread through this work is the use of mass spectrometry to follow how cells respond to their surroundings when they decide to grow or change identity.
Robitaille now works at Thermo Fisher Scientific in San Jose, California, as a Senior Product Applications Specialist for mass spectrometry and proteomics.

highlights.ROB2013: First author: used quantitative phosphoproteomics to show that mTORC1 activates pyrimidine synthesis through S6 kinase and CAD.

Robitaille AM.note: Thermo Fisher page header says 'Senior Product Marketing Manager' while the bio says 'Senior Product Applications Specialist'; the latter used. San Jose is not in canonical_locations; used '(San Jose, California, USA)'. Pronoun 'him' removed.

Jenoe P.lab_name: Proteomics Core Facility, Biozentrum, University of Basel (Basel, Switzerland)
Jenoe P.role: Protein chemist who ran mass spectrometry and protein sequencing at the Biozentrum Basel for decades and contributed protein analysis to many mTOR studies from Michael Hall's lab
Jenoe P.sub: Proteomics Core Facility, Biozentrum, University of Basel (PubMed affiliation to 2022) · Department of Biochemistry, Biozentrum, University of Basel (1995)
story: Many discoveries about mTOR depend on identifying proteins and the phosphate tags on them, and that is the job of mass spectrometry. Paul Jenö is a co-author of the 2017 Cancer Cell study in this Atlas (GUR2017) from Michael Hall's lab. In a mouse model where too much mTOR signalling causes fatty liver that turns into liver cancer, the team found that mTORC2, the second mTOR complex, drives the production of fatty acids and sphingolipids, a class of membrane fats. Blocking either kind of fat synthesis prevented tumours in the mice, and in human liver cancer samples high lipid synthesis went together with mTORC2 activity.

Jenö has worked on protein analysis at the Biozentrum since at least the 1990s. A 1995 paper with Jenö as first author, from the Department of Biochemistry, described a simple method to digest proteins inside polyacrylamide gels to obtain internal sequences, a step that became routine in protein identification. Later papers list Jenö at the Biozentrum's Proteomics Core Facility, usually together with Suzette Moes, on studies ranging from mTOR signalling to maternal blood markers of Down syndrome (2009) and prostate cancer (2022).

PubMed shows more than 100 papers under this name, many of them from Michael Hall's lab, including the 2013 phosphoproteomics study that linked mTORC1 to pyrimidine synthesis. A current position after 2022 could not be confirmed.

highlights.GUR2017: Co-author: provided protein mass spectrometry for the mouse study showing that mTORC2 drives liver cancer through lipid synthesis.

Jenoe P.note: Name spelled 'Jenö' in PubMed; 'full' changed from 'Paul Jenoe' to 'Paul Jenö'. PubMed lists Jenö and Suzette Moes on ROB2013 (PMID 23429704) too; curator may link that study to both profiles. Other Atlas records without affiliation remain unlinked.

Moes S.lab_name: Proteomics Core Facility, Biozentrum, University of Basel (Basel, Switzerland)
Moes S.role: Protein scientist at the Biozentrum Basel's proteomics facility who, with Paul Jenö, carried out mass spectrometry for many mTOR studies from Michael Hall's lab
Moes S.sub: Proteomics Core Facility, Biozentrum, University of Basel (PubMed records 1995–2022)
story: Suzette Moes is a co-author of the 2017 Cancer Cell study in this Atlas (GUR2017) from Michael Hall's lab. In mice in which too much mTOR signalling causes fatty liver that progresses to liver cancer, the team found that mTORC2 drives the production of fatty acids and sphingolipids, a class of membrane fats. Blocking either kind of fat synthesis prevented tumours, and in human liver cancer samples high lipid synthesis went together with mTORC2 activity.

Moes's role in this and many other Basel papers was protein analysis by mass spectrometry. PubMed shows Moes working with Paul Jenö from at least 1995, when the two published a method for digesting proteins inside polyacrylamide gels to read their internal sequences, through work at the Biozentrum's proteomics facility on topics from mTOR signalling to maternal blood markers of Down syndrome (2009).
The PubMed record under this name and Basel runs to 2022. A current position could not be confirmed.

highlights.GUR2017: Co-author: contributed protein mass spectrometry to the mouse study showing that mTORC2 drives liver cancer through lipid synthesis.

Hagiwara A.lab_name: Hall Lab, Biozentrum, University of Basel (Basel, Switzerland)
Hagiwara A.role: First author of a 2012 mouse study from Michael Hall's lab showing that liver mTORC2 tells the liver that the animal has eaten, by switching on sugar breakdown and fat production
Hagiwara A.sub: Biozentrum, University of Basel, Michael N. Hall group (at the time of the study, 2012)
story: After a meal, insulin tells the liver to stop making glucose and to start burning it and storing the extra as fat. Asami Hagiwara was first author of the 2012 Cell Metabolism study in this Atlas (HAG2012), from Michael Hall's lab in Basel, which asked what role mTORC2, the second mTOR complex, plays in that switch. The team deleted rictor, a core part of mTORC2, only in the liver of mice.

In fed mice without liver mTORC2, the kinase Akt lost its activating phosphate at serine 473, and the enzyme glucokinase and the fat-making regulator SREBP1c became less active. The liver kept making glucose while glycolysis (sugar breakdown) and fat synthesis fell, as if it could not sense that the animal had eaten. The mice developed high blood sugar and high insulin with low blood lipids. In liver cells lacking mTORC2, an always-active form of Akt2 restored both sugar breakdown and fat production, while extra glucokinase restored only the sugar side, so Akt is the main route from mTORC2 to these outputs. The study, in mice and mouse liver cells, placed mTORC2 at the centre of the liver's response to insulin.
PubMed lists Hagiwara at the Biozentrum of the University of Basel on this paper. No other paper could be tied to this person with confidence, so the later career is not known.

highlights.HAG2012: First author: showed in mice that liver mTORC2 activates glycolysis and fat synthesis through Akt, glucokinase and SREBP1c.

Hagiwara A.note: Previous profile used 'her'; pronoun removed because no source states it.
